diagnostic_evidence.quote: This ensures that such an optimal trajectory does not intersect $S$.

issues.failure_explanation: The paper claims the potential V acts as a barrier in the posed optimal control problem so that optimal trajectories avoid S, and that the resulting equations are 'modified Euler's equations'. In the posed problem every admissible motion satisfies div v = 0 with fixed endpoints, hence φ(·,t) ∈ Diff_vol(Ω) maps Ω onto Ω with unit Jacobian; the change of variables y = φ(x,t) (the paper's own identity (change:variables)) gives ∫_Ω V(φ(x,t))dx = ∫_Ω V(y)dy for all t. The potential term of (first:functional) is therefore the constant ⟨V⟩ on the whole feasible set: the minimization is independent of V and no minimizer is influenced by the obstacle. Consistently, the derived equation (mod:eulereq) is dynamically identical to (eulereq): (v, p) solves it iff (v, p−V) solves Euler's equation, since ∇V is a gradient absorbed by the constraint-determined pressure; moreover the force +grad V in the stated equation points toward S (V grows toward it), i.e., attractive rather than the 'repulsion' the Remark announces. The V-terms in the necessary conditions arise only because the proof varies φ through maps that are not volume-preserving, i.e., outside the admissible class 𝒞 along which δ⟨V∘φ⟩ = ∫∇V·η = 0. What the paper claims (a barrier shaping optimal fluid motion, avoidance of S, pressure control) is thus not established by anything in the source.

failure_location.quote: Here $V$ denotes a potential function used to avoid certain region in $\Omega$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a repair must reformulate the problem so that the potential influences the objective on the feasible set (e.g., potential evaluated on tagged material trajectories, time-dependent obstacle, or a domain with the obstacle region removed), re-derive the optimality system for that formulation, and drop the claim that (mod:eulereq) constitutes modified dynamics.
issues.overall_effect: The central advertised mechanism — obstacle avoidance and pressure control via the artificial potential (abstract, Section 1, the Remark, Section 4, Section 5) — is unsupported: the optimal control problem coincides with Arnold's geodesic problem, Theorem th2's equation is a pressure reparametrization of the Euler equations with no new dynamics, and the simulations cannot evidence potential-induced avoidance. The formal statements th1/th2 survive only as gauge restatements of the unmodified Euler equations.
issues.title: Obstacle-avoidance objective is invariant along admissible motions; the 'modified Euler equation' is only a pressure gauge
issues.why_classification: Every source-supported resolution abandons the advertised obstacle-avoidance/pressure-control mechanism and requires a new problem formulation with a new derivation; no comparable version of the central claim survives, so the issue is serious.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof's displayed first variation is the correct differential of the functional as written (whose potential term is +⟨V∘φ⟩). Extracting the δφ-coefficient and setting it to zero gives (Tv∘φ)^Tπ + ∂tπ + grad V∘φ = 0, i.e., ∂tπ = −(Tv∘φ)^Tπ − grad V∘φ; the theorem and the proof's conclusion instead assert +grad V∘φ, an invalid final inference. As written, the functional is the (negative) Hamilton–Pontryagin integrand of the optimal control problem with cost ½⟨v,v⟩ − ⟨V∘φ⟩, not of the posed cost (first:functional). Propagating the corrected sign through the proof of Theorem th2 changes its conclusion to ∂_t v + (v·grad)v = −grad(p+V) rather than −grad(p−V); the stated sign also makes the potential force attractive toward the obstacle, contradicting the announced repulsion.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Flip the sign of the potential term in the definition of the extended action functional (write ⟨k div v − V∘φ⟩ instead of ⟨k div v + V∘φ⟩), which is also the sign matching the posed cost (first:functional); with that single change the displayed variation matches Theorem th1 and the derivation of Theorem th2 goes through verbatim.
issues.overall_effect: Theorem th1's third optimality equation is not established for the action functional as defined, and Theorem th2's equation (mod:eulereq) inherits the inverted sign of the potential force; the repulsive interpretation in the Remark is inconsistent with the stated equation.
issues.title: Sign error in the π-equation of Theorem th1, propagated to th2's modified Euler equation
issues.why_classification: A one-sign local correction (in the functional's potential term, or equivalently in the two theorems' V-terms and the proof's last display) makes all computations and both stated theorems correct; no substantive claim or guarantee is lost.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: may result in a discrete vector field with discrete divergence, even though we depart from divergence-free initial conditions
The color map shows the value of the discrete divergence at each point.

issues.failure_explanation: The stated initial field has divergence ∂_x u + ∂_y v = sin x sin y + cos x cos y = cos(x−y), which is not identically zero (it equals 1 on the line x = y). The experiment therefore does not depart from divergence-free initial conditions as asserted, so the premise 'we depart from divergence-free initial conditions' and the divergence color maps of Figures 1–2 are unsupported at the outset: the simulated flow is not an incompressible one even before discretization error.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the initial data by a genuinely divergence-free field (e.g., the Taylor–Green field u = sin x cos y, v = −cos x sin y) or correct the stated claim; the integration-and-projection pipeline and its interpretation then apply unchanged.
issues.overall_effect: The reported numerical experiment starts from an inadmissible (divergent) state; the simulation's value as evidence for the incompressible modified Euler dynamics is unreliable.
issues.title: Simulation's stated initial condition is not divergence-free
issues.why_classification: A local replacement of the initial data by a genuinely divergence-free field restores the stated premise; the pipeline, its guarantees, and its qualitative reading survive unchanged.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: We assume from now on  that $\Omega$ has a boundary and the tangencial component of $v$ vanishes at the boundary.
Our assumption is the minimal requirement to satisfy Stokes theorem in the proof of the main result as well as for numerical simulation purposes.

issues.failure_explanation: The paper imposes, 'from now on', a domain with boundary on which the tangential velocity vanishes, explicitly motivating this by the numerical simulations and using it to discard the boundary term in the first-variation argument. The reported simulations instead identify the border points of the square (a periodic torus, hence no boundary), and the prescribed initial velocity does not vanish there (u(0,y,0) = −sin y ≠ 0). The numerics therefore do not instantiate the setting in which the necessary conditions and (mod:eulereq) were derived, so the prose presenting them as evidence for the paper's results claims more than the setup supports.

failure_location.quote: The integration scheme uses an evenly spaced grid to integrate the vector field on the square $[0, 4\pi] \times [0, 4\pi]/\{0, 4\pi\}$ with discrete spacing between squares of $\Delta x = 4\pi/30$ and points lying in the border of the square identified.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: State the periodic boundary conditions explicitly and scope the numerical section as a periodic-domain experiment (or rerun with the assumed boundary condition); a contained restatement removes the inconsistency.
issues.overall_effect: The paper's only experiments are run outside its own declared regime; any claim linking the simulations to the theoretical guarantees of Sections 2–3 is unreliable.
issues.title: Numerical section violates the paper's standing boundary assumption
issues.why_classification: A local restatement of the domain/boundary conditions of the experiment, or of the claims made for it, removes the inconsistency without affecting any result, rate, or guarantee.
